text:
Radish.
DIFFICULTY
Easy
1/5
HARVEST SEASONS
Spring / Summer / Autumn

Fast-growing radishes provide mild, juicy spring roots and suit spare corners, window boxes, protected sowings or gaps between slower crops. Pick small red or red-white types young: heat, age and drought make them hot, woody, hollow or soft. Longer-growing winter radishes come in white, pink, black or red-white. Grate, pickle, braise or stir-fry them; autumn-lifted roots also store in cool, damp conditions.

Quick facts
Harvest

Apr – Nov

Germination

4–7 days

Row spacing

6 in. between rows

Yield (10 ft row)

Summer: 4 lb; winter: 10 lb

Ready in

Salad 3–6; winter 10–12 weeks from sowing

Sow

Salad types Mar–Aug. Winter and Japanese types Jul–early Aug.

Sowing depth

Salad: 1/2 in.; winter/oriental: about 3/4 in.

Plant spacing

Between plants: Salad 1–2 in.; winter/Japanese 6–8 in.

Extended season

Sow early salad varieties under cloches in favourable conditions.

Recommended varieties
SPRING/SUMMER
French Breakfast 3

A familiar long red-and-white summer radish. Sow small batches; pick promptly for crisp, mildly peppery roots.

SPRING/SUMMER
Cherry Belle

A round, bright-red salad radish for quick crops in beds or containers.

SPRING/SUMMER
Scarlet Globe

A round red summer radish for quick, repeat crops. Harvest young before roots become coarse.

WINTER
China Rose

A pink, long-rooted winter radish for autumn use, contrasting with round black storage types.

WINTER
Black Spanish Round

A black-skinned winter radish with firm white flesh, grown for large autumn roots, not quick summer crops.

Key risks
Checked growth / poor root quality

Turnips, swedes and radishes need steady, quick growth.

Flea beetle

Tiny beetles pepper seedling leaves with holes and can check young crops.

Bolting

Winter radishes sown before July may flower before forming usable roots.

Cabbage root fly

Late and winter radishes are often tunnelled by cabbage root fly maggots, especially after May sowings.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
78
ROOT CROPS

Sun in spring; light shade in summer.

Hot, dry conditions make roots hotter and woodier.

Thin only where needed.

Pull the largest roots first and let smaller ones grow on.

Do not sow winter radishes too early.

They need to grow steadily into autumn, not bolt in summer.

Soil & preparation
Use rich, damp soil with a little compost and a fine tilth for rapid, tender growth.
Spring sun; light summer shade. Lime acid soil if needed. Winter types need humus-rich drainage.
Sowing & planting
Sow salad radishes
Leave room to grow
Sow 

Scatter seed thinly along a short drill and cover lightly. For a small patch, broadcast and rake in. Repeat salad sowings fortnightly while conditions stay cool. Use the deeper sowing and wider final spacing for winter radishes.

Looking after the crop
Keep rows weed-free and evenly moist, especially as roots swell. Uninterrupted growth gives crisp, mild roots; dry checks make them hot, woody or pithy.
Thin only where needed. Pick the largest summer roots first and let smaller ones grow on, without leaving any too long.
Protect young leaves from flea beetle with fine mesh or fleece. Clear quick crops promptly for the next crop.
Follow later sowing dates for winter radishes: early sowings may flower in summer instead of forming autumn roots.
Harvesting & storage
Pick spring and summer radishes small, crisp and mild; harvest French Breakfast types before they become finger-thick and tough.
Spring varieties often take 40–50 days; the quickest take 3–4 weeks in good conditions. Pull surplus roots before they turn woody or hollow.
Lift winter radishes in October–November before hard frost, or leave hardy kinds in the ground where frost is mild. Store lifted roots cool and damp, for example in sand.
Pests & diseases
Problem	What to look for	What to do
Flea beetle	Shot-holed leaves.	Keep moist; use fine mesh.
Bolting	Early flowers; poor roots.	Sow winter radishes from July onwards.
Cabbage root fly	Roots tunnelled by maggots.	Use mesh; trim minor root damage.
Woody or hollow roots	Hot, woody or hollow roots.	Water evenly; thin and harvest promptly.
Acid soil	Poor growth in acid soil.	Test soil; lime only where needed.
Slugs and snails	Chewed seedlings; slime trails.	Check after dark; hand-pick around seedlings.
Final tips

Sow winter radishes in July or early August, not spring.

Clear quick crops promptly for the next crop.

VEGETABLE GUIDES

79
